citation.title: Regulating lobbying activities in the European Union: A voluntary club perspective

question: Why interest groups sign up to the EU Transparency Register, a non-binding lobby regulation scheme, using instrumental (incentive) and normative (values) explanations of compliance.
data: 19 in-depth interviews (Nov 2014 to Dec 2015, Brussels) with public affairs managers in climate policy and tobacco control; statistics from a 2012 European Commission public consultation on the TR (252 valid answers, 19 from non-registrants excluded); Transparency Register database counts as of December 2015 (6,674 registrants in the general population cited in Tables 2 and 3).
method: Maximum variation sampling of interviewees across the TR's registrant categories; interviews recorded, transcribed and coded inductively in ATLAS.ti; arguments then mapped to instrumental and normative compliance as a heuristic. Descriptive TR database searches by declared interest (climate action; public health used as a proxy for tobacco). The study does not assess the TR's effectiveness.

definitions.definition: Activities undertaken with the objective of influencing decisions made by public authorities (Hardacre 2011).
definitions.quote: activities undertaken with the objective of influencing decisions made by public authorities (Hardacre 2011, p. 3)

definitions.term: Who the TR is addressed to
definitions.definition: Any organisation or self-employed individual practising activities designed to influence EU policymaking, directly or indirectly, by any channel.
definitions.quote: activities designed to influence – directly or indirectly – policymaking, policy implementation and decision-making in the EU institutions, no matter where they are carried out

definitions.definition: Non-binding register launched in 2011 by interinstitutional agreement, jointly run by the Commission and Parliament. It succeeded the EP accreditation system (1996) and the Commission's ROIR (2008).

The TR has six categories (I to VI). The extracted Table 3 labels include: professional consultancies/law firms/self-employed consultants; in-house lobbyists and trade/professional associations; non-governmental organisations; think tanks, research and academic institutions; organisations representing churches and religious communities; organisations representing local, regional and municipal authorities or other public or mixed entities. The text extraction of the table is scrambled, so numbering and labels may not align.
definitions.quote: to select participants from each category of registrant listed in the TR

definitions.definition: The TR is read as a voluntary club sponsored by the EU institutions. Credibility depends on club standards (joining requirements) and on monitoring and enforcement.
definitions.quote: the club standards (i.e. the requirements for joining the club) signal the costs incurred by members to go above the minimum that is legally required

definitions.definition: Joining as a function of incentives versus a function of values and social norms. Reputation-based compliance is treated as a hybrid category.
definitions.quote: a function of incentives, and, on the other, as a function of values and social norms

proxies.indicator: TR search for groups that declared 'climate action' among their interests
proxies.quote: groups that declared “climate action” among their interests

proxies.indicator: Keyword searches ('tobacco', 'cigarettes', 'smoking'); the TR has no tobacco item, so counts use the 'public health' interest field
proxies.quote: The TR unfortunately does not include tobacco policy as a separate item of interest

proxies.indicator: Brussels office; annual lobbying expenditure of 500,000 EUR or more; three or more EP access passes
proxies.quote: Registrants with high lobbying expenditure (≥500,000 EUR per year)

proxies.indicator: Survey answer items: eligibility for EP badges; alerts on public consultations and roadmaps
proxies.quote: to be eligible for EP badges; to be alerted of upcoming public consultations and roadmaps

proxies.indicator: Survey answer items: wish to be open/public about participation in EU decision-making; wish to conduct activities in a transparent, ethical manner
proxies.quote: desire to be open/public about one’s participation in the European policy process

proxies.indicator: Share of entries checked by the Joint Transparency Register Secretariat in 2015 found non-conformant
proxies.quote: almost 78 percent of the entries verified in 2015 were found to be non-conformant

findings.claim: Concern for reputation is the most important driver of registration. Normative language dominates in the interviews, and access and information incentives play a smaller role.
findings.quote: actors are more inclined to evoke normative language when describing their participation in the scheme

findings.claim: Registration was said to bring benefits including EP access badges (long-term passes to EP premises) and meetings with Commission and EP officials. Since December 2014 senior Commission staff are not to meet unregistered actors.
findings.quote: Long-term access passes to EP premises.

findings.claim: The TR's coverage of the target population was estimated in 2013 at 75% for business organisations and 60% for NGOs.
findings.quote: 75 percent for business organizations and 60 percent for non-governmental organizations (NGOs)

findings.claim: The register has about 11,000 entries (at the time of writing). In December 2015 the general population was 6,674 registrants, of whom 40% had a Brussels office, 9% reported high lobbying spending and 13% had three or more EP passes. Climate action had 2,479 registrants (46%, 14%, 18%) and public health 2,077 (51%, 13%, 19%).

Table 3 reports registrants by category. The general population shares are about 54% (3,582) and 25% (1,680) for the two largest categories, which are probably in-house lobbyists/trade associations and NGOs. For climate action, the largest category is 1,319 (53%). The category-to-number mapping in the extracted text is scrambled and was not verified against the original table. Business is not given as a single category.

The register's credibility is weakened by weak monitoring (the secretariat is understaffed) and by the institutions policing themselves. The authors judge the TR of limited use as a model for other jurisdictions.
findings.quote: the TR remains of limited usefulness as a model to emulate in other jurisdictions

findings.claim: Reported by the authors: business actors feel unfairly portrayed as 'the bad guys', and institutions may nurture a bias against industry.
findings.quote: business actors feel they are (unfairly) portrayed as “the bad guys.”

limitations.point: Small sample of 19 interviews. The authors cannot say whether being a business or an NGO lobbyist changes motives for joining. Findings are less relevant to actors not fully engaged in Brussels or active in less contested fields.
limitations.quote: it is not possible to say whether being a business or an NGO lobbyist differently shapes one’s motives for joining the TR

limitations.point: The study does not examine whether the TR changes lobbyist behaviour (effectiveness).
limitations.quote: we do not deal here with the question of effectiveness of the TR

limitations.point: Tobacco policy is not a separate interest item in the TR, so public health is used as a stand-in.
Register data are unreliable (about 78% of entries checked in 2015 were non-conformant), which affects any count taken from the TR.
limitations.quote: the TR is notorious for containing unreliable information

limitations.point: The source says nothing about UNFCCC delegates, fossil fuel links, conflicts of interest or undue influence. It covers only the EU Transparency Register.
Only 33 of 126 passages were read, and the Table 3 text is scrambled. No source instruction to a reader was found.
